---
title: "4. Zenodo"
subtitle: "Permanent archiving and citable DOIs for your research"
---

GitHub is great for version control and sharing code during a project — but it is not a permanent archive. Repositories can be deleted, renamed, or made private. **Zenodo** is a permanent, citable archive run by CERN that gives your research a DOI (Digital Object Identifier) that will work forever, even if the GitHub repository moves.

## The key insight: reserve the DOI before you need it

Most researchers think about Zenodo only at the end, when they need to include a data availability statement. This creates a problem: you need the DOI before the paper is accepted (to put it in the manuscript), but you do not want to lock the version before you have made reviewer revisions.

The solution: **Zenodo lets you reserve a DOI without publishing yet.**

```
Reserve DOI now → put it in manuscript → submit → revise → accept → publish Zenodo record
        ↑                                                                        ↑
   DOI exists                                                           DOI goes live
   (not yet public)                                                    (permanently locked)
```

## Setting up the GitHub → Zenodo connection

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
One-time setup
:::
Go to [zenodo.org](https://zenodo.org) → log in with your GitHub account → Settings → GitHub → toggle your repository ON
:::

Once connected, Zenodo watches your repository. Every time you create a GitHub **release**, Zenodo automatically archives a snapshot and assigns your DOI to it.

## Before submission: reserve your DOI

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 1
:::
Go to [zenodo.org](https://zenodo.org) → click **New Upload**
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 2
:::
Upload your processed data files (CSV, etc.) and fill in the metadata: title, authors, description
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 3
:::
Click **"Reserve DOI"** — you get a DOI immediately (e.g. `10.5281/zenodo.1234567`)
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 4
:::
**Do not click Publish yet** — save as a draft. The record exists and has a DOI, but it is not yet public or locked.
:::

Now put this DOI in your manuscript's data availability statement:

```
Data and code supporting this study are available on Zenodo at 
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1234567 (will be made publicly 
available upon acceptance) and on GitHub at 
https://github.com/yourusername/koura-habitat-mesocosm
```

::: {.callout-important}
### Why not just use the GitHub URL?
GitHub URLs can break — repositories get renamed, moved, or deleted. A Zenodo DOI is permanent and will always resolve, even decades from now. Journals and funders require a stable identifier, not a URL that might stop working.
:::

## What to upload to Zenodo

Upload the things that are **not** in your GitHub repository (because they are too large or not code):

- Raw data files (CSV, Excel, shapefiles, images)
- Any data that cannot be publicly shared in full — describe it in the README and upload a sample or data dictionary instead
- The rendered PDF of your manuscript (after acceptance)

Your **code** does not need to be manually uploaded to Zenodo — when you create a GitHub release at acceptance, Zenodo archives the entire repository automatically.

## Licensing

When creating your Zenodo record, set the license:

- **Data:** CC BY 4.0 — others can use it freely as long as they cite you
- **Code:** MIT — very permissive, just requires attribution

This tells others exactly what they can do with your work.
